Completing the Square: Free Response

5 questions in parts, 55 points in total. Work each one out on paper, taking a hint if you get stuck. When you have an answer, reveal the answer to check it, and the full solution only if you still want it. The rubric is there so you can mark your own work.

Free response · work it on paper Question 1 of 5
  1. 1

    1. One rewrite, two questions . Foundational, 9 points. Question 1 of 5.

    Foundational 9 pts

    The quadratic x2−9x+4x^2 - 9x + 4x2−9x+4 has an odd middle coefficient, so the constant that completes its square is not a whole number. Nothing in the method minds that. This question performs the change of form once, and then puts the finished expression to two uses that look unrelated.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Rewrite x2−9x+4x^2 - 9x + 4x2−9x+4 as a squared binomial plus a constant. Then expand your form back to standard form and confirm it returns the expression you started from.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Solve x2−9x+4=0x^2 - 9x + 4 = 0x2−9x+4=0 exactly, by isolating the square and extracting the root. Report both solutions, and substitute one of them into the original equation to confirm it.

      Carry your own answer forward Continue from the completed form you produced in part A, whatever it came out as. The marks here are for isolating the square, for attaching the plus-or-minus, and for reporting two exact solutions, not for the rewrite itself.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Standard form answers neither of the two questions above directly. Say what the single rewrite in part A made available in each case, and explain why one finished expression can serve two purposes that look unrelated.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 3 points

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 4

      This question is one computation followed by two readings of what it produced. Do the computation once and carefully, then resist the urge to start it over again for the second reading.

    2. Hint 2 of 4 · Part A

      Half of an odd number is not a whole number, and the method does not care. Halve the coefficient of xxx as a fraction, square that fraction, and keep the loose constants over one common denominator.

    3. Hint 3 of 4 · Part B

      Do not expand or distribute anything here. Move the loose constant across first, so that the square is standing alone before any root is taken, and remember what a lone root leaves out.

    4. Hint 4 of 4 · Part C

      Count how many separate terms carry an xxx in the quadratic as given, and how many carry one in a squared binomial plus a constant. The difference between those two counts is what both of the earlier parts were quietly exploiting.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    x2−9x+4=(x−92)2−654x^2 - 9x + 4 = \left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{65}{4}x2−9x+4=(x−29​)2−465​.

    • (x−4.5)2−16.25(x - 4.5)^2 - 16.25(x−4.5)2−16.25, the same two numbers written as decimals

    Part B

    x=9+652x = \dfrac{9 + \sqrt{65}}{2}x=29+65​​ and x=9−652x = \dfrac{9 - \sqrt{65}}{2}x=29−65​​, written together as x=9±652x = \dfrac{9 \pm \sqrt{65}}{2}x=29±65​​.

    • x=92±652x = \tfrac{9}{2} \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{65}}{2}x=29​±265​​, the same two numbers with the halving carried out on each piece

    Part C

    The rewrite collects every occurrence of xxx into one square. Read as it stands, the square is never negative, so the vertex, axis and minimum are visible with no work; set equal to zero, that same lone square can be undone with a plus-or-minus. Standard form displays neither directly and is not ready for a root.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The variable part is x2−9xx^2 - 9xx2−9x, so the coefficient to halve is −9-9−9, half of it is −92-\tfrac{9}{2}−29​, and squaring that gives the completing constant:

    (−92)2=814.\left(-\tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{81}{4}.(−29​)2=481​.

    Add it and subtract it in the same line, so that the appearance of the expression changes and its value does not:

    x2−9x+4=(x2−9x+814)−814+4.x^2 - 9x + 4 = \left(x^2 - 9x + \tfrac{81}{4}\right) - \tfrac{81}{4} + 4.x2−9x+4=(x2−9x+481​)−481​+4.

    The bracket is the perfect square (x−92)2\left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2(x−29​)2, since half of −9-9−9 is −92-\tfrac{9}{2}−29​ and that is the number the square carries. The loose constants combine over a denominator of 444, writing 444 as 164\tfrac{16}{4}416​:

    −814+164=−654.-\tfrac{81}{4} + \tfrac{16}{4} = -\tfrac{65}{4}.−481​+416​=−465​.

    So the change of form is

    x2−9x+4=(x−92)2−654.x^2 - 9x + 4 = \left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{65}{4}.x2−9x+4=(x−29​)2−465​.

    Check it by expanding. (x−92)2=x2−9x+814\left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 = x^2 - 9x + \tfrac{81}{4}(x−29​)2=x2−9x+481​, and subtracting 654\tfrac{65}{4}465​ leaves x2−9x+164x^2 - 9x + \tfrac{16}{4}x2−9x+416​, which is x2−9x+4x^2 - 9x + 4x2−9x+4. The two expressions agree for every xxx, which is what makes this a rewrite rather than an approximation.

    Part B

    Nothing is distributed or expanded here. Put the completed form in place of the left-hand side:

    (x−92)2−654=0.\left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{65}{4} = 0.(x−29​)2−465​=0.

    Isolate the square by adding 654\tfrac{65}{4}465​ to both sides:

    (x−92)2=654.\left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{65}{4}.(x−29​)2=465​.

    The right-hand side is positive, so the root of both sides carries a plus-or-minus. Writing only the positive root would quietly throw the second solution away:

    x−92=±652.x - \tfrac{9}{2} = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt{65}}{2}.x−29​=±265​​.

    The denominator 444 is a perfect square, so its root is 222; the numerator 65=5⋅1365 = 5 \cdot 1365=5⋅13 is not, so 65\sqrt{65}65​ does not simplify and the answer stays exact rather than decimal. Adding 92\tfrac{9}{2}29​ to both sides:

    x=92±652=9±652.x = \tfrac{9}{2} \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{65}}{2} = \dfrac{9 \pm \sqrt{65}}{2}.x=29​±265​​=29±65​​.

    Check the first one. With x=9+652x = \dfrac{9 + \sqrt{65}}{2}x=29+65​​,

    x2=81+1865+654=146+18654,x^2 = \dfrac{81 + 18\sqrt{65} + 65}{4} = \dfrac{146 + 18\sqrt{65}}{4},x2=481+1865​+65​=4146+1865​​,

    while −9x=−162−18654-9x = \dfrac{-162 - 18\sqrt{65}}{4}−9x=4−162−1865​​ and 4=1644 = \dfrac{16}{4}4=416​. The two terms carrying 65\sqrt{65}65​ cancel exactly, and the plain numbers give 146−162+16=0146 - 162 + 16 = 0146−162+16=0, so the total is 000 and the value satisfies the equation.

    Part C

    Count the places xxx appears. In x2−9x+4x^2 - 9x + 4x2−9x+4 it appears in two terms, of different degree, and there is no way to gather them: there is no single xxx to solve for, and no way to see how the two terms behave against each other as xxx moves.

    The completed form has xxx in exactly one place, inside the square:

    x2−9x+4=(x−92)2−654.x^2 - 9x + 4 = \left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{65}{4}.x2−9x+4=(x−29​)2−465​.

    That single occurrence is what both readings exploit, in opposite directions.

    Read the form as it stands. A real square is never negative, so (x−92)2≥0\left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 \ge 0(x−29​)2≥0, with equality exactly when x=92x = \tfrac{9}{2}x=29​. The whole expression is therefore at least −654-\tfrac{65}{4}−465​, and equals it only there. So the vertex is (92, −654)\left(\tfrac{9}{2},\ -\tfrac{65}{4}\right)(29​, −465​), the axis of symmetry is x=92x = \tfrac{9}{2}x=29​, and the smallest value the expression takes is −654-\tfrac{65}{4}−465​. No equation was solved to get any of that.

    Now set the same form equal to zero instead. Because xxx occurs once, the square can be moved onto one side by itself, and undoing a square is a move that exists: take the root of both sides and attach a plus-or-minus. That move is simply not available while xxx sits in two terms at once, which is why the standard form has to be left behind first.

    So the two payoffs are not two techniques that happen to share a first step. They are one structural fact, that every xxx has been collected into a single square, used first for reading and then for solving.

    In one line

    x2−9x+4=(x−92)2−654x^2 - 9x + 4 = \left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{65}{4}x2−9x+4=(x−29​)2−465​, which expands back to the expression it came from. Setting that equal to zero gives (x−92)2=654\left(x - \tfrac{9}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{65}{4}(x−29​)2=465​, so x=9±652x = \dfrac{9 \pm \sqrt{65}}{2}x=29±65​​, and substituting either value returns 000. One rewrite serves both jobs because it collects every xxx into a single square: read as it stands, that square is never negative, so the expression is at least −654-\tfrac{65}{4}−465​ and the vertex is (92, −654)\left(\tfrac{9}{2},\ -\tfrac{65}{4}\right)(29​, −465​); set equal to zero, the same lone square can be undone with a plus-or-minus. Standard form carries xxx in two terms, so it displays neither reading directly and is not ready for a square root to be taken.

    Another way: Multiply through first, and keep the fractions out until the end

    Fractions can be postponed by working with the equation rather than the expression. Multiply x2−9x+4=0x^2 - 9x + 4 = 0x2−9x+4=0 through by 444:

    4x2−36x+16=0.4x^2 - 36x + 16 = 0.4x2−36x+16=0.

    The leading term is now a perfect square, and 4x2−36x=(2x)2−18(2x)4x^2 - 36x = (2x)^2 - 18(2x)4x2−36x=(2x)2−18(2x), so completing the square in the quantity 2x2x2x needs half of −18-18−18, squared, which is 818181:

    (2x−9)2=81−16=65.(2x - 9)^2 = 81 - 16 = 65.(2x−9)2=81−16=65.

    So 2x−9=±652x - 9 = \pm\sqrt{65}2x−9=±65​ and x=9±652x = \dfrac{9 \pm \sqrt{65}}{2}x=29±65​​, the same two numbers with no fraction written until the last line.

    When it is worth it When an odd middle coefficient makes the fractions unpleasant and only the SOLUTIONS are wanted. It works on an equation, which has a second side to multiply, and it does not produce the vertex form, so it cannot then be read for the vertex or the minimum.

    Rewrite x2−11x+3x^2 - 11x + 3x2−11x+3 as a squared binomial plus a constant, solve x2−11x+3=0x^2 - 11x + 3 = 0x2−11x+3=0 exactly, and state the smallest value the expression can take and where it occurs.

    The answer

    x2−11x+3=(x−112)2−1094x^2 - 11x + 3 = \left(x - \tfrac{11}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{109}{4}x2−11x+3=(x−211​)2−4109​, so x=11±1092x = \dfrac{11 \pm \sqrt{109}}{2}x=211±109​​, and the smallest value of the expression is −1094-\tfrac{109}{4}−4109​, taken at x=112x = \tfrac{11}{2}x=211​.

    Half of −11-11−11 is −112-\tfrac{11}{2}−211​, and squaring gives 1214\tfrac{121}{4}4121​. Adding and subtracting it,

    x2−11x+3=(x−112)2−1214+124=(x−112)2−1094.x^2 - 11x + 3 = \left(x - \tfrac{11}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{121}{4} + \tfrac{12}{4} = \left(x - \tfrac{11}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{109}{4}.x2−11x+3=(x−211​)2−4121​+412​=(x−211​)2−4109​.

    Expanding back gives x2−11x+1214−1094=x2−11x+3x^2 - 11x + \tfrac{121}{4} - \tfrac{109}{4} = x^2 - 11x + 3x2−11x+4121​−4109​=x2−11x+3, so the rewrite holds.

    Setting it to zero and isolating the square,

    (x−112)2=1094,x−112=±1092,\left(x - \tfrac{11}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{109}{4}, \qquad x - \tfrac{11}{2} = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt{109}}{2},(x−211​)2=4109​,x−211​=±2109​​,

    so x=11±1092x = \dfrac{11 \pm \sqrt{109}}{2}x=211±109​​, and 109109109 is prime, so the root does not simplify.

    Reading the same form instead of solving it, the square is never negative and is zero only at x=112x = \tfrac{11}{2}x=211​, so the smallest value of the expression is −1094-\tfrac{109}{4}−4109​, taken there.

    Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 4

      A factored-out coefficient has not gone anywhere; it is parked outside a bracket. Everything that ends up inside that bracket has to be multiplied by it on the way back out.

    2. Hint 2 of 4 · Part A

      Only the two terms carrying an xxx go inside the bracket. Once they are in, the coefficient of xxx is a fraction, so halve the fraction and square the fraction, and watch what pulling out a negative does to its sign. Coming back out, check what the bracket is holding besides the square.

    3. Hint 3 of 4 · Part B

      A square of a real number is at least zero. Multiply that comparison by a negative number and it turns around, and turning it around is exactly what decides between a highest point and a lowest one.

    4. Hint 4 of 4 · Part C

      Two independent checks catch a slip like this without redoing the method: expand a finished form back to standard form, or evaluate the two versions at one convenient input and compare what they give.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    g(x)=−4(x−54)2+294g(x) = -4\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 + \tfrac{29}{4}g(x)=−4(x−45​)2+429​.

    • −4(x−1.25)2+7.25-4(x - 1.25)^2 + 7.25−4(x−1.25)2+7.25, the same numbers written as decimals

    Part B

    Vertex (54, 294)\left(\tfrac{5}{4},\ \tfrac{29}{4}\right)(45​, 429​), axis x=54x = \tfrac{5}{4}x=45​. The leading coefficient is negative, so the vertex is the highest point: the maximum value is 294\tfrac{29}{4}429​, and the range is g(x)≤294g(x) \le \tfrac{29}{4}g(x)≤429​.

    Part C

    Line 3. The 555 was distributed to the square but not to the constant beside it inside the bracket, which should become −20-20−20. The line must read 5(x−2)2−20+3=5(x−2)2−175(x - 2)^2 - 20 + 3 = 5(x - 2)^2 - 175(x−2)2−20+3=5(x−2)2−17, so the smallest value is −17-17−17, not −1-1−1.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Factor −4-4−4 out of the x2x^2x2 and xxx terms only. The loose constant carries no xxx, so it stays outside the bracket:

    −4x2+10x+1=−4(x2−52x)+1.-4x^2 + 10x + 1 = -4\left(x^2 - \tfrac{5}{2}x\right) + 1.−4x2+10x+1=−4(x2−25​x)+1.

    Dividing 101010 by −4-4−4 gives −52-\tfrac{5}{2}−25​, and the sign is worth a pause: pulling out a negative flips the sign of the middle term inside the bracket.

    Inside, the coefficient of xxx is −52-\tfrac{5}{2}−25​, half of it is −54-\tfrac{5}{4}−45​, and squaring gives 2516\tfrac{25}{16}1625​. Add and subtract that inside the bracket:

    −4(x2−52x+2516−2516)+1=−4((x−54)2−2516)+1.-4\left(x^2 - \tfrac{5}{2}x + \tfrac{25}{16} - \tfrac{25}{16}\right) + 1 = -4\left(\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 - \tfrac{25}{16}\right) + 1.−4(x2−25​x+1625​−1625​)+1=−4((x−45​)2−1625​)+1.

    Now the step the whole method turns on. The −4-4−4 multiplies everything the bracket holds, the subtracted constant included:

    −4⋅(−2516)=254,-4 \cdot \left(-\tfrac{25}{16}\right) = \tfrac{25}{4},−4⋅(−1625​)=425​,

    so the finished form is

    g(x)=−4(x−54)2+254+1=−4(x−54)2+294.g(x) = -4\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 + \tfrac{25}{4} + 1 = -4\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 + \tfrac{29}{4}.g(x)=−4(x−45​)2+425​+1=−4(x−45​)2+429​.

    Expand back to check. −4(x2−52x+2516)=−4x2+10x−254-4\left(x^2 - \tfrac{5}{2}x + \tfrac{25}{16}\right) = -4x^2 + 10x - \tfrac{25}{4}−4(x2−25​x+1625​)=−4x2+10x−425​, and −254+294=44=1-\tfrac{25}{4} + \tfrac{29}{4} = \tfrac{4}{4} = 1−425​+429​=44​=1, which returns −4x2+10x+1-4x^2 + 10x + 1−4x2+10x+1.

    Part B

    Read the finished form against the shape a(x−h)2+ka(x - h)^2 + ka(x−h)2+k. Here a=−4a = -4a=−4, h=54h = \tfrac{5}{4}h=45​ and k=294k = \tfrac{29}{4}k=429​, so the vertex is (54, 294)\left(\tfrac{5}{4},\ \tfrac{29}{4}\right)(45​, 429​) and the axis of symmetry is the vertical line x=54x = \tfrac{5}{4}x=45​.

    Which kind of extreme point that vertex is follows from two facts and no testing. First, a real square is never negative:

    (x−54)2≥0for every real x.\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 \ge 0 \quad \text{for every real } x.(x−45​)2≥0for every real x.

    Second, multiplying both sides by the negative number −4-4−4 reverses the comparison:

    −4(x−54)2≤0.-4\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 \le 0.−4(x−45​)2≤0.

    Adding 294\tfrac{29}{4}429​ to both sides gives g(x)≤294g(x) \le \tfrac{29}{4}g(x)≤429​ for every real xxx. Equality needs the square to be zero, which happens only at x=54x = \tfrac{5}{4}x=45​. So the vertex is the highest point of the graph, and the maximum value is 294\tfrac{29}{4}429​, attained exactly once.

    That last word decides the range. The value 294\tfrac{29}{4}429​ is reached, so it belongs to the range; and the square can be made as large as you like by taking xxx far from 54\tfrac{5}{4}45​, so −4-4−4 times it runs down without end. The outputs therefore fill everything from 294\tfrac{29}{4}429​ downwards: the range is g(x)≤294g(x) \le \tfrac{29}{4}g(x)≤429​.

    Notice that the sign of the leading coefficient did two jobs at once. It turned the comparison around, which made the vertex a maximum, and it is the same sign that opens the parabola downward.

    Part C

    Work down the lines and stop at the first that fails.

    Line 1 is correct: the 555 comes out of the x2x^2x2 and xxx terms and the loose constant stays outside. Line 2 is correct too: inside the bracket the coefficient of xxx is −4-4−4, half of it is −2-2−2, squaring gives 444, and adding and subtracting that turns x2−4xx^2 - 4xx2−4x into (x−2)2−4(x - 2)^2 - 4(x−2)2−4.

    Line 3 is the first line that fails. The 555 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it, and the bracket holds two things:

    5((x−2)2−4)=5(x−2)2−20.5\left((x - 2)^2 - 4\right) = 5(x - 2)^2 - 20.5((x−2)2−4)=5(x−2)2−20.

    The student multiplied the square by 555 and carried the other piece out untouched. Written correctly the line reads

    5(x−2)2−20+3=5(x−2)2−17,5(x - 2)^2 - 20 + 3 = 5(x - 2)^2 - 17,5(x−2)2−20+3=5(x−2)2−17,

    so the smallest value of the expression is −17-17−17, taken at x=2x = 2x=2, not −1-1−1.

    Two checks expose this without running the method again. The first is to expand the student's form:

    5(x−2)2−1=5x2−20x+20−1=5x2−20x+19,5(x - 2)^2 - 1 = 5x^2 - 20x + 20 - 1 = 5x^2 - 20x + 19,5(x−2)2−1=5x2−20x+20−1=5x2−20x+19,

    which is not the expression that was handed in, so the rewrite cannot be an identity. The second is to evaluate both versions at a single convenient input. At x=2x = 2x=2 the original gives

    5(4)−20(2)+3=20−40+3=−17,5(4) - 20(2) + 3 = 20 - 40 + 3 = -17,5(4)−20(2)+3=20−40+3=−17,

    while the student's form gives 5(0)−1=−15(0) - 1 = -15(0)−1=−1. One input is enough to convict, because a correct rewrite has to agree everywhere, so a single disagreement settles it.

    In one line

Its vertex is (54, 294)\left(\tfrac{5}{4},\ \tfrac{29}{4}\right)(45​, 429​) and its axis of symmetry is x=54x = \tfrac{5}{4}x=45​. Because a real square is never negative and the leading coefficient is negative, −4(x−54)2≤0-4\left(x - \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 \le 0−4(x−45​)2≤0 with equality only at x=54x = \tfrac{5}{4}x=45​, so the vertex is the highest point, the maximum value is 294\tfrac{29}{4}429​, and the range is g(x)≤294g(x) \le \tfrac{29}{4}g(x)≤429​. It stops there: it never produces the completed form, so it cannot then be isolated and solved, and it does not exhibit the range as a consequence of a square being nonnegative, though the range does still follow once the vertex and the direction of opening are known.

    Application 13 pts

    Answer and solution

    The answer

    Part A

    w=8w = 8w=8 and w=15w = 15w=15, both allowed: a plot 888 metres deep by 303030 along the wall, and one 151515 metres deep by 161616 along the wall. Each uses all the fencing.

    No width achieves it. The greatest area available is smaller than the target, and setting the area equal to the target gives (w−232)2=−314\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{31}{4}(w−223​)2=−431​.     Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Name the sides before writing anything down. Two sides run away from the wall, each of length www metres, and one side runs along the wall; the wall itself is not fenced. So the fencing is spent on three sides:

    2w+ℓ=46,2w + \ell = 46,2w+ℓ=46,

    where ℓ\ellℓ is the length in metres of the side along the wall. That single equation in two unknowns is exactly what lets one of them be eliminated:

    ℓ=46−2w.\ell = 46 - 2w.ℓ=46−2w.

    The area is the product of the two dimensions, so substituting for ℓ\ellℓ leaves a function of www alone:

    A(w)=wℓ=w(46−2w)=−2w2+46w,A(w) = w\ell = w(46 - 2w) = -2w^2 + 46w,A(w)=wℓ=w(46−2w)=−2w2+46w,

    measured in square metres.

    Not every number is a possible www. A side of length zero or less is not a side, so w>0w > 0w>0; and the side along the wall must also be positive, which needs 46−2w>046 - 2w > 046−2w>0, that is w<23w < 23w<23. So the plots that can actually be built are those whose www lies strictly between 000 and 232323 metres. The restriction comes from the situation, not from the algebra, which would happily accept any number at all.

    Part B

    Complete the square on A(w)=−2w2+46wA(w) = -2w^2 + 46wA(w)=−2w2+46w. Both terms carry a www, so factor −2-2−2 out of both:

    A(w)=−2(w2−23w).A(w) = -2\left(w^2 - 23w\right).A(w)=−2(w2−23w).

    Inside, half of −23-23−23 is −232-\tfrac{23}{2}−223​ and squaring gives 5294\tfrac{529}{4}4529​, so add and subtract that inside the bracket:

    A(w)=−2((w−232)2−5294).A(w) = -2\left(\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{529}{4}\right).A(w)=−2((w−223​)2−4529​).

    Distribute the −2-2−2 across both pieces, the subtracted constant included:

    A(w)=−2(w−232)2+5292.A(w) = -2\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{529}{2}.A(w)=−2(w−223​)2+2529​.

    Now read it. The square is never negative and −2-2−2 is negative, so the first term is at most zero and therefore

    A(w)≤5292for every w,A(w) \le \tfrac{529}{2} \quad \text{for every } w,A(w)≤2529​for every w,

    with equality exactly when the square is zero, at w=232=11.5w = \tfrac{23}{2} = 11.5w=223​=11.5. That width lies inside the permitted range, so it is a plot the club can really build, which had to be checked rather than assumed.

    The largest area is therefore 5292=264.5\tfrac{529}{2} = 264.52529​=264.5 square metres. The dimensions are 11.511.511.5 metres for each of the two sides running from the wall and 46−2(11.5)=2346 - 2(11.5) = 2346−2(11.5)=23 metres along the wall. Check both records: 11.5×23=264.511.5 \times 23 = 264.511.5×23=264.5 square metres, and the fencing used is 11.5+11.5+23=4611.5 + 11.5 + 23 = 4611.5+11.5+23=46 metres, all of it.

    Part C

    Set the completed form equal to the target:

    −2(w−232)2+5292=240.-2\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{529}{2} = 240.−2(w−223​)2+2529​=240.

    Move the constant across and divide by −2-2−2, so that the square is standing alone. Since 5292−240=529−4802=492\tfrac{529}{2} - 240 = \tfrac{529 - 480}{2} = \tfrac{49}{2}2529​−240=2529−480​=249​,

    −2(w−232)2=−492,(w−232)2=494.-2\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{49}{2}, \qquad \left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{49}{4}.−2(w−223​)2=−249​,(w−223​)2=449​.

    The right-hand side is positive, so take the root of both sides and attach the plus-or-minus:

    w−232=±72.w - \tfrac{23}{2} = \pm\tfrac{7}{2}.w−223​=±27​.

    That gives w=232+72=15w = \tfrac{23}{2} + \tfrac{7}{2} = 15w=223​+27​=15 and w=232−72=8w = \tfrac{23}{2} - \tfrac{7}{2} = 8w=223​−27​=8.

    Both lie strictly between 000 and 232323, so both describe plots that can be built, and the two plots are genuinely different rather than the same one written twice. At w=8w = 8w=8 the side along the wall is 46−16=3046 - 16 = 3046−16=30 metres, and 8×30=2408 \times 30 = 2408×30=240 square metres. At w=15w = 15w=15 it is 46−30=1646 - 30 = 1646−30=16 metres, and 15×16=24015 \times 16 = 24015×16=240 square metres. Each uses 8+8+30=468 + 8 + 30 = 468+8+30=46 metres and 15+15+16=4615 + 15 + 16 = 4615+15+16=46 metres of fencing respectively, all of it.

    So the club really does have two choices, and nothing here rules a value out. A negative width would have been rejected, and so would a width big enough to leave no wall side, but neither happens: in this situation any target area strictly between zero and the greatest available is met at two different widths, one on each side of the width that gives the greatest area, and here both of them fit.

    Part D

    Two routes, and they agree.

    The first needs no equation at all. Part B established that the area never exceeds 5292=264.5\tfrac{529}{2} = 264.52529​=264.5 square metres, and 264.5264.5264.5 is less than 280280280. A quantity that never exceeds 264.5264.5264.5 cannot equal 280280280. That is the entire argument, and it is available only because the completed form states the ceiling outright; the standard form −2w2+46w-2w^2 + 46w−2w2+46w states no ceiling anywhere.

    The second route runs the algebra anyway, because what it produces is the point of the part. Setting the area equal to the target,

    −2(w−232)2+5292=280.-2\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{529}{2} = 280.−2(w−223​)2+2529​=280.

    Writing 280280280 as 5602\tfrac{560}{2}2560​ and moving the constant across,

    −2(w−232)2=560−5292=312,-2\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{560 - 529}{2} = \tfrac{31}{2},−2(w−223​)2=2560−529​=231​,

    and dividing by −2-2−2 isolates the square:

    (w−232)2=−314.\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{31}{4}.(w−223​)2=−431​.

    A real square is never negative, and the right-hand side is negative, so no real number www satisfies this. There is nothing further to do and nothing has gone wrong. The method finished, and what it delivered is the information that the target cannot be met.

    That is the point worth keeping. An isolated square equal to a negative number is an answer, not a stuck calculation, and here it says something concrete about fencing: no rectangular plot of this kind can enclose 280280280 square metres with 464646 metres of fence, whatever its dimensions. The club must either accept at most 264.5264.5264.5 square metres, build something that is not a rectangle, or buy more fencing.

    In one line

    With the wall as one side, 2w2w2w plus the side along the wall uses all 464646 metres, so A(w)=w(46−2w)=−2w2+46wA(w) = w(46 - 2w) = -2w^2 + 46wA(w)=w(46−2w)=−2w2+46w for www strictly between 000 and 232323. Completing the square gives A(w)=−2(w−232)2+5292A(w) = -2\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{529}{2}A(w)=−2(w−223​)2+2529​, so the largest area is 264.5264.5264.5 square metres, from a plot 11.511.511.5 metres deep and 232323 metres along the wall. For 240240240 square metres the isolated square is (w−232)2=494\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{49}{4}(w−223​)2=449​, giving w=8w = 8w=8 and w=15w = 15w=15: two genuinely different plots, 888 by 303030 metres and 151515 by 161616 metres, both buildable. For 280280280 square metres the same step gives (w−232)2=−314\left(w - \tfrac{23}{2}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{31}{4}(w−223​)2=−431​, and a real square is never negative, so no rectangular plot of this kind encloses that much; the completed form said as much in one line, since 264.5264.5264.5 is already the ceiling.

    Another way: Factor the target equation instead, when the numbers happen to be friendly

    The 240240240 square metre target can also be met by factoring, because this particular target leaves whole numbers behind. Dividing −2w2+46w=240-2w^2 + 46w = 240−2w2+46w=240 through by −2-2−2 gives

    w2−23w+120=0,w^2 - 23w + 120 = 0,w2−23w+120=0,

    and two numbers with product 120120120 and sum −23-23−23 are −8-8−8 and −15-15−15, so

    (w−8)(w−15)=0.(w - 8)(w - 15) = 0.(w−8)(w−15)=0.

    The Zero Product Property then gives the same two widths.

    When it is worth it Only when the target happens to produce a factorization over the integers, which is a property of the numbers rather than of the method. It is quicker there, but it is a search, and it has nothing to offer on the 280280280 square metre target or on any target that leaves an irrational width, which is exactly why the completed form is the route that always works.

    Reasoning 12 pts

    The expression 2x2+5x−22x^2 + 5x - 22x2+5x−2 has no factorization into linear factors with integer coefficients: the search for a suitable integer pair runs out of candidates. This question is about what happens next, and about how much the method that follows actually promises.

Support your verdict by taking x2+5x+9=0x^2 + 5x + 9 = 0x2+5x+9=0 all the way through, and state the three things an isolated square can report.

      An equation has two sides, so the whole equation may be divided through by the leading coefficient before anything else happens. An expression has only one side, and needs that coefficient factored out instead.

    3. Hint 3 of 4 · Part B

      One of these routes works through a list of candidates and the other works through a sequence of arithmetic steps. Ask what each is entitled to conclude at the moment it finishes, and what a finished list leaves open.

    4. Hint 4 of 4 · Part C

      The claim runs two separate things together: arriving at the form, and what the form then reports. Push the supporting equation all the way to an isolated square and look hard at the number standing on the right of it.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    x=−5+414x = \dfrac{-5 + \sqrt{41}}{4}x=4−5+41​​ and x=−5−414x = \dfrac{-5 - \sqrt{41}}{4}x=4−5−41​​, written together as x=−5±414x = \dfrac{-5 \pm \sqrt{41}}{4}x=4−5±41​​.

    • x=−54±414x = -\tfrac{5}{4} \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{41}}{4}x=−45​±441​​, the same two numbers with the division carried out on each piece

    Part B

    A factor search only ever tests finitely many integer pairs; here every pair fails, so it stops with no verdict about the roots. Completing the square asks nothing that can be answered no: halving a number and squaring it always returns a number, so the route always reaches a finished form.

    Part C

    It does not follow. The method always delivers a completed form; what that form then reports is a separate matter it settles rather than assumes. For x2+5x+9=0x^2 + 5x + 9 = 0x2+5x+9=0 the isolated square equals −114-\tfrac{11}{4}−411​, so there is no real solution. A positive value gives two, zero gives exactly one, a negative value gives none.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    This is an equation, not a bare expression, so it has a second side and may be divided through by the leading coefficient. Every term goes:

    x2+52x−1=0.x^2 + \tfrac{5}{2}x - 1 = 0.x2+25​x−1=0.

    Move the constant to the right, leaving the variable terms alone and ready to be completed:

    x2+52x=1.x^2 + \tfrac{5}{2}x = 1.x2+25​x=1.

    Half of 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​ is 54\tfrac{5}{4}45​, and squaring gives 2516\tfrac{25}{16}1625​. Add it to BOTH sides, which is the equation's version of adding and subtracting in the same line:

    (x+54)2=1+2516=4116.\left(x + \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 = 1 + \tfrac{25}{16} = \tfrac{41}{16}.(x+45​)2=1+1625​=1641​.

    The right-hand side is positive, so there are two real solutions and the root carries a plus-or-minus. The denominator 161616 is a perfect square while 414141 is prime, so

    x+54=±414,x=−5±414.x + \tfrac{5}{4} = \pm\tfrac{\sqrt{41}}{4}, \qquad x = \dfrac{-5 \pm \sqrt{41}}{4}.x+45​=±441​​,x=4−5±41​​.

    Check the first. With x=−5+414x = \dfrac{-5 + \sqrt{41}}{4}x=4−5+41​​,

    x2=25−1041+4116=33−5418,x^2 = \dfrac{25 - 10\sqrt{41} + 41}{16} = \dfrac{33 - 5\sqrt{41}}{8},x2=1625−1041​+41​=833−541​​,

    so 2x2=33−54142x^2 = \dfrac{33 - 5\sqrt{41}}{4}2x2=433−541​​, while 5x=−25+54145x = \dfrac{-25 + 5\sqrt{41}}{4}5x=4−25+541​​. The terms carrying the root cancel and 33−254=2\dfrac{33 - 25}{4} = 2433−25​=2, so 2x2+5x−2=2−2=02x^2 + 5x - 2 = 2 - 2 = 02x2+5x−2=2−2=0.

    Part B

    Start with what each route promises, because that is where they differ, not in how hard the arithmetic is.

    An integer factor search promises a finite check and nothing more. For 2x2+5x−22x^2 + 5x - 22x2+5x−2 you look for integers filling (2x+m)(x+n)(2x + m)(x + n)(2x+m)(x+n), which needs mn=−2mn = -2mn=−2 and 2n+m=52n + m = 52n+m=5. There are four integer pairs with product −2-2−2, and the middle coefficients they produce are

    −3,3,0,0,-3, \quad 3, \quad 0, \quad 0,−3,3,0,0,

    none of which is 555. The list is exhausted and the search stops exactly there. It has established something real, that no integer pair works, but that is not a solution and does not point at one. Its promise was only ever to test candidates, so when every candidate fails it has nothing left to say about the roots.

    Completing the square makes no such bargain, because it never asks a question that could be answered 'no candidates left'. Every step is a computation rather than a search: halve the coefficient of xxx, square the result, add and subtract it, and tidy up. Halving a real number always returns a real number, and squaring one always returns a real number, so the finished form is reached whatever the coefficients are, this quadratic included.

    The two therefore fail in incomparable ways. One can run out of candidates; the other has no candidates to run out of. That is the sense in which completing the square never fails, and it is why this lesson sits after factoring rather than beside it.

    The answer from part A shows the gap concretely. Its two numbers are irrational, and any factorization into linear factors with integer coefficients would have forced them to be rational, so they were out of the factor search's reach before it started.

    Part C

    Take the claim apart. Its premise is true and its conclusion does not follow from it.

    What never fails is the rewrite. Given any ax2+bx+cax^2 + bx + cax2+bx+c with a≠0a \ne 0a=0, every step of the method is a computation, so the steps always finish, and they always finish in the same shape: one square, times a constant, plus a constant. That much is guaranteed in advance.

    What the finished form then says is a separate question, and the form is what answers it. Isolate the square and the equation reads

    (x−h)2=k(x - h)^2 = k(x−h)2=k

    for some number kkk that the coefficients decide. Exactly one of three things is true of kkk. If k>0k > 0k>0 there are two real solutions, x=h±kx = h \pm \sqrt{k}x=h±k​. If k=0k = 0k=0 those two collapse into the single solution x=hx = hx=h. If k<0k < 0k<0 there is no real solution at all, because a real square is never negative.

    So the method is a reporter, not a guarantor. It always reaches the crossroads; it never promises which way the crossroads points.

    The supporting equation makes that concrete. For x2+5x+9x^2 + 5x + 9x2+5x+9, half of 555 is 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​ and squaring gives 254\tfrac{25}{4}425​, so

    x2+5x+9=(x+52)2−254+9=(x+52)2+114.x^2 + 5x + 9 = \left(x + \tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 - \tfrac{25}{4} + 9 = \left(x + \tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 + \tfrac{11}{4}.x2+5x+9=(x+25​)2−425​+9=(x+25​)2+411​.

    Setting that equal to zero and isolating the square,

    (x+52)2=−114,\left(x + \tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{11}{4},(x+25​)2=−411​,

    which no real xxx satisfies. The method did not fail on this equation; it succeeded, and what it produced is the information that the equation has no real solution. Read the very same form the other way and it says the smallest value of x2+5x+9x^2 + 5x + 9x2+5x+9 is 114\tfrac{11}{4}411​, comfortably above zero, which is the same fact seen from the other side: the graph sits entirely above the axis, so there is nothing for it to cross.

    The repair to the claim is to say precisely what never fails. Reaching the completed form never fails. Finding a real root is not something any method could promise, because for some equations there is nothing there to find.

    In one line

    Dividing 2x2+5x−2=02x^2 + 5x - 2 = 02x2+5x−2=0 through by 222 and completing the square gives (x+54)2=4116\left(x + \tfrac{5}{4}\right)^2 = \tfrac{41}{16}(x+45​)2=1641​, so x=−5±414x = \dfrac{-5 \pm \sqrt{41}}{4}x=4−5±41​​, and substituting either value returns 000. An integer factor search could never have produced these: it tests only the four integer pairs with product −2-2−2, whose middle coefficients are −3-3−3, 333, 000 and 000, so it exhausts its list and stops with no verdict, whereas halving and squaring a coefficient always returns a number and so always reaches a finished form. But the classmate's conclusion does not follow from that. What never fails is reaching the form; the form then reports one of three things, according to the number the isolated square is left equal to: two real solutions when it is positive, exactly one when it is zero, and none when it is negative. Here x2+5x+9=0x^2 + 5x + 9 = 0x2+5x+9=0 becomes (x+52)2=−114\left(x + \tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{11}{4}(x+25​)2=−411​, and a real square is never negative, so that equation has no real solution.

    5. What the identity forces, and what it does not . Reasoning, 11 points. Question 5 of 5.

    Reasoning 11 pts

    Everything in this lesson rests on one line, (x+p)2=x2+2px+p2(x + p)^2 = x^2 + 2px + p^2(x+p)2=x2+2px+p2, read from right to left. This question asks first what that line forces, then what the form it produces settles about a graph, and finally what it does not settle.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Let bbb and ddd be real numbers. Prove that there is a real number ppp with x2+bx+d=(x+p)2x^2 + bx + d = (x + p)^2x2+bx+d=(x+p)2 for every xxx if and only if d=(b2)2d = \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2d=(2b​)2. Prove both directions separately, and say what your argument establishes about how many such ppp there can be.

      Complete the derivation Each line should follow from the one above it. Say what lets you take each step. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate claims: 'two quadratics with the same leading coefficient and the same coefficient of xxx, but different constant terms, always share an axis of symmetry, and never have the same number of real solutions.' One half of that is right.     Hints

    One at a time, each one a step further than the last. Take only as many as you need.

    1. Hint 1 of 4

      An 'if and only if' is two claims wearing one coat, and only one of them is the direction the method leans on every day. Write down what each direction may assume and what it must deliver before proving either.

    2. Hint 2 of 4 · Part A

      Two polynomials agree at every input only when their matching coefficients agree. Comparing the coefficient of xxx first pins the inner number down completely, before the constant term is looked at at all.

    3. Hint 3 of 4 · Part B

      Nothing here needs the three letters in the form to be any particular numbers. Substitute the two inputs into the form as it stands and watch what the subtraction inside the bracket leaves behind in each case.

    4. Hint 4 of 4 · Part C

      A half saying 'always' and a half saying 'never' are refuted by quite different instances. Work out, for each half separately, exactly what one pair of quadratics would have to do to break it, before going hunting for that pair. Then fix the first two coefficients, move the constant term a little rather than a lot, and watch whether anything reaches zero or passes it.

    That is every hint for this question.

    Answer and solution

    Check your answer first. If it is wrong, go back to your paper: the worked solution will still be here.

    The answer

    Part A

    Both directions hold. Matching against x2+2px+p2x^2 + 2px + p^2x2+2px+p2 forces 2p=b2p = b2p=b and p2=dp^2 = dp2=d, hence p=b2p = \tfrac{b}{2}p=2b​ and d=(b2)2d = \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2d=(2b​)2; conversely that value of ddd makes the trinomial (x+b2)2\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2(x+2b​)2 exactly. The ppp is unique, since 2p=b2p = b2p=b has one solution.

    Part B

    Both sides come out as as2+kas^2 + kas2+k, since (h+s)−h=s(h + s) - h = s(h+s)−h=s and (h−s)−h=−s(h - s) - h = -s(h−s)−h=−s, and squaring destroys the sign. So the graph takes equal values at inputs equally far either side of hhh, which makes x=hx = hx=h its axis of symmetry.

    Part C

    The first half is right, the second is false. 2x2+3x−12x^2 + 3x - 12x2+3x−1 and 2x2+3x−52x^2 + 3x - 52x2+3x−5 each have two real solutions. Changing the constant term slides the number the isolated square is left equal to, and the count changes only when that slide changes its status among positive, zero and negative.

    Not what you got? Look for the slip on your own paper before you open the solution. Finding it yourself is worth more than reading it.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The claim is an 'if and only if', so there are two things to prove and they are not the same thing.

    First direction, that the condition is necessary. Suppose x2+bx+d=(x+p)2x^2 + bx + d = (x + p)^2x2+bx+d=(x+p)2 for some real ppp and for every xxx. Expanding the right-hand side,

    x2+bx+d=x2+2px+p2.x^2 + bx + d = x^2 + 2px + p^2.x2+bx+d=x2+2px+p2.

    Two polynomials agree at every xxx only if their matching coefficients agree, so the xxx terms give b=2pb = 2pb=2p and the constants give d=p2d = p^2d=p2. (If you would rather not appeal to that principle, substitute x=0x = 0x=0 to get d=p2d = p^2d=p2, then x=1x = 1x=1 to get 1+b+d=1+2p+p21 + b + d = 1 + 2p + p^21+b+d=1+2p+p2, which with d=p2d = p^2d=p2 leaves b=2pb = 2pb=2p.) The first equation forces p=b2p = \tfrac{b}{2}p=2b​, and substituting into the second gives

    d=p2=(b2)2.d = p^2 = \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2.d=p2=(2b​)2.

    So no other constant is available: this direction rules every other value of ddd out.

    Second direction, that the condition is sufficient. Suppose d=(b2)2d = \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2d=(2b​)2. Take p=b2p = \tfrac{b}{2}p=2b​ and expand:

    (x+b2)2=x2+2⋅b2⋅x+(b2)2=x2+bx+d.\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 = x^2 + 2 \cdot \tfrac{b}{2} \cdot x + \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 = x^2 + bx + d.(x+2b​)2=x2+2⋅2b​⋅x+(2b​)2=x2+bx+d.

    So such a ppp exists whenever the condition holds. The two directions together make the condition exact rather than merely one that happens to work.

    How many such ppp can there be? The first direction pinned it down with no choice left: 2p=b2p = b2p=b is a linear equation with exactly one solution. So ppp is unique, and the familiar instruction to halve the coefficient of xxx is not one recipe among several but the only one there is, which is why the method needs no guessing anywhere.

    One consequence is worth noticing on the way out. Since ddd must equal (b2)2\left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2(2b​)2, and a real square is never negative, no trinomial x2+bx+dx^2 + bx + dx2+bx+d with d<0d < 0d<0 is a perfect square, whatever bbb may be.

    Part B

    Completing the square puts every quadratic into the shape f(x)=a(x−h)2+kf(x) = a(x - h)^2 + kf(x)=a(x−h)2+k, so anything proved about that shape is a statement about every quadratic at once.

    Evaluate at the two inputs in turn. At x=h+sx = h + sx=h+s the bracket is (h+s)−h=s(h + s) - h = s(h+s)−h=s, so

    f(h+s)=as2+k.f(h + s) = as^2 + k.f(h+s)=as2+k.

    At x=h−sx = h - sx=h−s the bracket is (h−s)−h=−s(h - s) - h = -s(h−s)−h=−s, so

    f(h−s)=a(−s)2+k=as2+k,f(h - s) = a(-s)^2 + k = as^2 + k,f(h−s)=a(−s)2+k=as2+k,

    using (−s)2=s2(-s)^2 = s^2(−s)2=s2. That is where the whole proof lives: squaring destroys the sign, so the two inputs are indistinguishable to the form.

    The two right-hand sides are identical, so f(h+s)=f(h−s)f(h + s) = f(h - s)f(h+s)=f(h−s) for every real sss. Nothing was assumed about aaa, hhh, kkk or sss, so this holds for every quadratic and every distance, including s=0s = 0s=0, where it says nothing at all, and negative sss, which merely swaps the two inputs over.

    What that means for the graph: any two inputs the same distance either side of hhh produce the same output, so the graph is carried onto itself by reflection in the vertical line x=hx = hx=h. That line is the axis of symmetry.

    It is worth seeing how much the change of form did here. In standard form this statement is a computation with terms to cancel; in the completed form it is two substitutions and the observation that a square ignores a sign.

    Part C

    Write both quadratics in the same completed shape and the two halves come apart cleanly. Fix the leading coefficient and the coefficient of xxx, and let the constant term be ccc. Completing the square gives

    ax2+bx+c=a(x−h)2+k,ax^2 + bx + c = a(x - h)^2 + k,ax2+bx+c=a(x−h)2+k,

    where hhh is decided by the first two coefficients alone: it comes from halving the coefficient of xxx after aaa has been factored out, a step the constant term never enters. Changing ccc shifts kkk by the same amount and leaves hhh exactly where it was.

    So the first half is right, and for a reason rather than by coincidence: the axis of symmetry is x=hx = hx=h, and hhh does not depend on ccc. Part B is what turns that into a statement about the graph.

    The second half is false. Take

    f(x)=2x2+3x−1,g(x)=2x2+3x−5,f(x) = 2x^2 + 3x - 1, \qquad g(x) = 2x^2 + 3x - 5,f(x)=2x2+3x−1,g(x)=2x2+3x−5,

    which share their first two coefficients and differ in the constant term. Factoring 222 out of the variable terms, half of 32\tfrac{3}{2}23​ is 34\tfrac{3}{4}43​ and squaring gives 916\tfrac{9}{16}169​, so both begin from 2(x+34)2−982\left(x + \tfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 - \tfrac{9}{8}2(x+43​)2−89​ and then carry their own constant. Setting each to zero and isolating the square,

    (x+34)2=1716and(x+34)2=4916.\left(x + \tfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \tfrac{17}{16} \quad \text{and} \quad \left(x + \tfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \tfrac{49}{16}.(x+43​)2=1617​and(x+43​)2=1649​.

    Both right-hand sides are positive, so each equation has two real solutions: x=−3±174x = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{4}x=4−3±17​​ for the first, and x=1x = 1x=1 or x=−52x = -\tfrac{5}{2}x=−25​ for the second, since ±74\pm\tfrac{7}{4}±47​ comes out exactly. Check the second pair in ggg: 2+3−5=02 + 3 - 5 = 02+3−5=0, and 252−152−5=0\tfrac{25}{2} - \tfrac{15}{2} - 5 = 0225​−215​−5=0. Two quadratics, the same first two coefficients, different constant terms, and the same count.

    What actually governs the count is the number the isolated square is left equal to. Moving the constant term slides that number, so it CAN change the count, but only when the slide changes which of positive, zero and negative that number is. Between these two quadratics the number moves from 1716\tfrac{17}{16}1617​ to 4916\tfrac{49}{16}1649​ and stays positive the whole way, so the count cannot change. Push the constant term far enough in the other direction and eventually the number reaches zero, where the two solutions collapse into one, and then goes negative, where there are none. Note that reaching zero is enough on its own: the count drops from two to one there, without the number having to pass through to the other side.

    The classmate's error is a common shape: treating a quantity that certainly moves as though moving were the same thing as changing what it reports.

    In one line

    x2+bx+dx^2 + bx + dx2+bx+d is a perfect square exactly when d=(b2)2d = \left(\tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2d=(2b​)2: matching against x2+2px+p2x^2 + 2px + p^2x2+2px+p2 forces 2p=b2p = b2p=b and p2=dp^2 = dp2=d in one direction, and that value of ddd builds (x+b2)2\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2(x+2b​)2 in the other, with the inner number unique because 2p=b2p = b2p=b has exactly one solution. For f(x)=a(x−h)2+kf(x) = a(x - h)^2 + kf(x)=a(x−h)2+k, both f(h+s)f(h + s)f(h+s) and f(h−s)f(h - s)f(h−s) reduce to as2+kas^2 + kas2+k, since squaring ignores the sign of the bracket, so the graph is carried onto itself by reflection in x=hx = hx=h, which is its axis of symmetry. The classmate's first half is right for exactly that reason, the axis being x=hx = hx=h whatever the constant term is; the second half is false, and 2x2+3x−12x^2 + 3x - 12x2+3x−1 beside 2x2+3x−52x^2 + 3x - 52x2+3x−5 settles it, since both complete from 2(x+34)2−982\left(x + \tfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 - \tfrac{9}{8}2(x+43​)2−89​ and leave isolated squares equal to 1716\tfrac{17}{16}1617​ and 4916\tfrac{49}{16}1649​, both positive, so each equation has two real solutions. What governs the count is the number the isolated square is left equal to, and moving the constant term changes the count only when it changes whether that number is positive, zero or negative.

    Rubric

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.

    Part A 4 points

    3

    Argues the two directions separately, so that the condition on the constant term is shown to be necessary as well as sufficient rather than only demonstrated in the direction the method uses. . Worth 3 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer

    1

    States what pins the inner number down, and concludes from that equation that no second value of it is available. . Worth 1 point.

    Part B 3 points

    2

    Evaluates the form at both shifted inputs and reduces each to the same expression, using explicitly that squaring the two opposite bracket values gives the same result. . Worth 2 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer

    1

    Says what equal outputs at inputs equidistant from the vertex mean for the shape of the graph, naming the line rather than restating the equation. . Worth 1 point.

    Part C 4 points

    2

    Produces a specific pair differing only in the constant term, and carries both far enough to settle the disputed half rather than asserting an outcome for it. . Worth 2 points.

    2

    Gives a reason for whichever half survives, drawn from where each of the three coefficients enters the completed form, so that the two halves are separated by an argument and not only by an example. . Worth 2 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer

    Try a similar problem (Optional)

    Same idea, different numbers. Work it on paper, then check yourself the same way.

    Decide whether this is true: two quadratics with the same leading coefficient and the same constant term, but different coefficients of xxx, never have the same number of real solutions. Settle it with a specific pair, carried far enough to be convincing.

    The answer

    False. 3x2+2x+73x^2 + 2x + 73x2+2x+7 and 3x2+4x+73x^2 + 4x + 73x2+4x+7 share a leading coefficient and a constant term, and their isolated squares come out equal to −209-\tfrac{20}{9}−920​ and −179-\tfrac{17}{9}−917​, both negative, so neither equation has any real solution and the two counts agree.

    It is false, and a pair with no real solutions at all settles it quickly. Take

    3x2+2x+7and3x2+4x+7,3x^2 + 2x + 7 \qquad \text{and} \qquad 3x^2 + 4x + 7,3x2+2x+7and3x2+4x+7,

    which share their leading coefficient and their constant term and differ in the middle. Dividing each equation through by 333 and completing the square, half of 23\tfrac{2}{3}32​ is 13\tfrac{1}{3}31​ and half of 43\tfrac{4}{3}34​ is 23\tfrac{2}{3}32​, so

    (x+13)2=−73+19=−209,(x+23)2=−73+49=−179.\left(x + \tfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{7}{3} + \tfrac{1}{9} = -\tfrac{20}{9}, \qquad \left(x + \tfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{7}{3} + \tfrac{4}{9} = -\tfrac{17}{9}.(x+31​)2=−37​+91​=−920​,(x+32​)2=−37​+94​=−917​.

    Both right-hand sides are negative, and a real square is never negative, so neither equation has a real solution. The counts agree, and the claim is refuted.

    The reason is the same as before. The middle coefficient certainly moves the number the isolated square is left equal to, but moving a number is not the same as changing whether it is positive, zero or negative.

Marking rubrics

Work every question first. Then mark your own paper against these, giving yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down.

1. One rewrite, two questions 9 points

Part A 3

  • Halves the coefficient of xxx and squares the result, then adds and subtracts that constant in the same line so that the value of the expression is left untouched. 2
  • Expands the finished form back to standard form and compares it term by term with the expression it started from. 1

Part B 3

  • Isolates the square before any root is taken, and attaches the plus-or-minus so that two solutions come out rather than one. 2
  • Reports both solutions in exact form, with no decimal rounding, and substitutes one of them into the original equation to confirm it returns zero. 1

Part C 3

  • Traces both uses back to the same structural feature of the completed form, rather than describing the two procedures one after the other as separate recipes. 3

2. Running the route with a coefficient outside 10 points

Part A 3

  • Factors the leading coefficient out of the x2x^2x2 and xxx terms only, leaving the loose constant outside the bracket, and halves the resulting inner coefficient as a fraction. 2
  • Multiplies the factored-out coefficient back across both pieces inside the bracket, the subtracted constant included, and verifies the finished form by expanding it. 1

Part B 3

  • Names the vertex, the axis of symmetry, the extreme value and the range, each read off the completed form rather than computed again from the standard form. 2
  • Argues which kind of extreme point the vertex is from the sign of the leading coefficient together with the fact that a real square is never negative, rather than asserting it from the shape of the graph. 1

Part C 4

  • Names the first line that fails, states exactly what was done to it, and writes that line as it should have read. 2
  • Backs the diagnosis with two independent checks, one expanding a finished form back to standard form and one evaluating the original expression and the student's version at the same input, and says why a single disagreeing input is enough. 2

  • Gives both arguments, one comparing the target against the greatest area the completed form allows and one carrying the equation through to an isolated square, and says why the number that square is left equal to settles the question outright. 3
  • Turns the verdict into a statement about the fencing the club actually has, rather than leaving it as a line of algebra. 1
